Achillea alpina.note: Leafy stems crowded with narrow, undivided, saw-toothed leaves 4 to 8 cm, like a comb, topped by a domed cluster of small white daisies with cream centres, each 0.8 to 1 cm with 6 to 12 short rays. It is recorded with the common yarrow's twice-cut leaf. The model is bare wires and ground ladders under a hovering white plate.

Achillea borealis.note: Feathery leaves cut so finely they look like green fur, at the base and all the way up the stems; each stem ends in a flat to domed white head 4 to 8 cm across of many tiny daisies. The model's flat white plate is recognisable. It hovers above the stalk tips, the stalks are bare, and the leaves are a few small ladders on the ground.

Acorus americanus.note: A fan of sword-shaped, bright yellow-green leaves with an off-centre midrib, and a finger-like yellow-green spike 4 to 8 cm long that juts out sideways at an angle from partway up a leaf-like stalk. The model is a dark tight column with no spike showing in June: the angled finger is the one thing that tells it from an iris or a cattail.

Actaea rubra.note: A bushy plant of large leaves divided two or three times into sharply toothed, lobed leaflets; a dense fluffy white ball of flowers 3 to 5 cm on a stalk above the leaves; then a tight cluster of glossy red berries on the same stalk. The model has plain oval leaflets, a tall thin column of specks, and berries scattered through the air around the plant.

Agastache foeniculum.note: Square stems with opposite, toothed, pointed oval leaves, pale beneath, each stem ending in a dense, fuzzy, solid blue-violet spike 3 to 10 cm long and 2 cm thick. The model's posture, opposite leaves and spike position are right. Its spikes are open strings of small dark and lilac dots, where the plant's are solid.

Agoseris glauca.note: A rosette of narrow lance leaves, blue-grey with a pale midrib, and leafless stalks each with one yellow dandelion-like head 3 cm across; a white puff ball after. The model's rosette and bare stalks are right in kind. The leaves are near black, not blue-grey, and the heads are small dark striped discs.

Agrimonia striata.note: A tall hairy stem with large leaves of 5 to 9 big, coarsely toothed leaflets and tiny ones between them, ending in a long slim wand of small bright yellow five-petalled flowers; nodding burs with hooked bristles. The model is two nearly bare stems with tiny ladder leaves and short strings of pale dots.

Alisma triviale.note: A tuft of long-stalked, oval, pointed leaves with parallel veins, and a tall stalk that branches in whorls, and those again in whorls, into a broad open pyramid dotted with small three-petalled white flowers. The model's leaves on stalks are right. Its flowers are a loose cloud of pale and dark flecks, not on branches, and the leaves are dark teal.

Allium cernuum.note: A small tuft of soft, narrow, grass-like leaves, and bare stalks that crook over at the top like a shepherd's hook, each hanging an open umbel of 8 to 30 pale pink to white bells. The model's tuft with a pink cluster on a stalk is the right kind. The head points up, not down, and half of it renders maroon.

Allium schoenoprasum.note: A dense tuft of round, hollow, blue-green tubes, with stalks each topped by one tight pompom 2 to 4 cm across of pink-mauve, papery, pointed flowers. The model's tuft with pink on stalks is the right kind. Its head is a loose spray of pink and maroon chips, not a ball, and the leaves are flat blades.

Alnus alnobetula.note: A dense many-stemmed shrub; shiny oval leaves with sharp fine teeth; long yellow catkins in spring; small woody cones that stay through winter. The model is thick sticks with leaf cards at the tips, and bare sticks in April with no catkins.

Alnus incana.note: A tall many-stemmed shrub or small tree with smooth grey bark; dull oval leaves, doubly toothed, deeply veined; long catkins on bare twigs in April; small woody cones all year. The model is the same sticks with leaf cards as Green Alder, and bare in April.

Amelanchier alnifolia.note: A dense thicket of slender grey stems, leafy throughout; oval leaves toothed above the middle, 3 to 5 cm; white five-petalled flowers with narrow petals all over it in May; purple-black berries in July. The model is a fan of thick square sticks from one point with a few large leaf cards at the tips; no flower shows in May and no berry in July.

Anaphalis margaritacea.note: White-woolly stems with narrow leaves, green above and white beneath, topped by a flat cluster of many pearly white papery globes 1 cm across, each with a small yellow centre; they dry in place and stay. The model has the grey leaf, drawn as a tower of long blades. Its flowers are a thin line of yellow specks drifting off above the plant: no white at all.

Anemonastrum canadense.note: Colonies knee high: long-stalked leaves cut into 3 to 5 sharply toothed parts, a ruff of stalkless leaves under each flower stalk, and white flowers 2.5 to 4 cm with a yellow centre held well above the leaves. Recorded 60 cm tall; the model is a flat mat a hand high with small white flowers lying on it.

Anemone cylindrica.note: A tuft of deeply cut leaves, a whorl of leaves partway up, and long bare stalks each with one greenish-white flower 2 cm; then the thimble it is named for, a narrow grey-green cylinder 2 to 4 cm tall that stays all summer and turns to wool. The model has round dark plates, flowers adrift from the stalks and no thimbles.

Anemone multifida.note: A tuft of leaves cut into many narrow fingers, a ruff of the same halfway up each hairy stem, and one flower 1.5 to 2.5 cm per stem: cream, yellow-green or deep magenta-red, round a green button; then a ball of white wool. The model has round dark plates for leaves and pink stars drifting in the air above the stalks.

Anemone virginiana.note: A tall plant with large, deeply three-parted, toothed leaves, a whorl of them halfway up the stem, and long bare stalks each with one white to greenish flower 2 to 3 cm; then an egg-shaped thimble that turns to cotton. The model's stems with white flowers on top are closest of the anemones; the leaves are dark round plates and there are no thimbles.

Antennaria microphylla.note: A dense silver-white mat of very small leaves under 1 cm, with stalks a hand high carrying tight clusters of small white to cream heads. The model's grey mound is the right colour. Its leaf plates are many times too large for a plant named for its small leaves, and the flowers are specks lying on the mound.

Antennaria neglecta.note: A flat mat of small spoon-shaped leaves, green above and white-woolly beneath, spreading by runners, with woolly stalks a hand high, each topped by a tight bunch of white fuzzy heads like a cat's paw. The model has the grey leaf colour, which helps. Its leaves are large angular plates in a mound and the flowers are pinpoint specks lying on it: no stalks, no paws.

Antennaria parvifolia.note: A flat silver mat of small spoon-shaped leaves in rosettes, with short woolly stalks each topped by a tight bunch of white, sometimes pink-tipped, fuzzy heads. The model's grey mound has the colour. The leaf plates are far too big and the flowers are specks lying on it, with no stalks.

Antennaria pulcherrima.note: The tall pussytoes: upright, white-woolly stems to 40 cm from a tuft of long, narrow, grey, erect basal leaves, with leaves up the stem, topped by a tight cluster of woolly heads in brown-tipped bracts. The model is a scatter of dark seed-sized flecks on the ground and two hair-thin wires, with dots hanging far above them. There is no plant.

Antennaria rosea.note: A grey-woolly mat of small leaves with slender stalks to 20 cm, each topped by a tight cluster of heads wrapped in rose-pink to deep pink papery bracts. The model is the same grey mound of plates as the other pussytoes with white specks: no pink, which is its name, and no stalks.

Apocynum androsaemifolium.note: A bushy, forking plant with reddish stems and opposite, drooping, blue-green oval leaves 5 to 8 cm; small pink bells striped deeper pink, in loose clusters at the branch tips; long thin paired pods. The model is a solid cone of leaf plates stacked like a pine cone, with flecks on top.

Aquilegia brevistyla.note: A mound of blue-green leaves, each divided twice into rounded, lobed leaflets like a meadow-rue, and slender stems with a few nodding flowers 2 cm: blue-purple sepals round cream-white petals with short hooked spurs. The model is six bare wires from a few tiny ladder leaves, with upright blue tubes off the stalk tips: no cream, no nodding.

Aralia nudicaulis.note: One leaf on a tall bare stalk, held flat like an umbrella: three branches, each with 3 to 5 broad, toothed, oval leaflets 8 to 12 cm; bronze when new, yellow in autumn. Beneath it, on its own short stalk from the ground, two to seven round balls of green-white flowers, then purple-black berries. The model is an upright stem of ladder leaves, with no flower or fruit recorded.

Arctostaphylos uva-ursi.note: A trailing evergreen mat of long woody stems closely set with small, leathery, spoon-shaped leaves 1 to 2.5 cm, dark glossy green, bronze-red in winter; small pink-tipped white urns in clusters at the shoot tips; bright red berries. The model is a flat star of pale angular plates, each several times the size of a leaf, with white specks.

Arnica chamissonis.note: Leafy stems with 5 to 10 pairs of grey-green lance leaves up the stem, no rosette at flowering, and several bright yellow daisies 4 to 5 cm at the top; it grows in patches. The model is a dark rosette of broad leaves with bare wires and two pale tan discs: the opposite of a plant named for its leafy stem.

Arnica fulgens.note: Tufts of narrow lance leaves, grey-green and ribbed, mostly at the base; each stem carries one bright yellow head 5 to 6 cm with an orange-yellow centre. The model's leaves are broad dark ovals flat on the ground and its heads hover above the stalk tips, dark from the side.

Artemisia campestris.note: A rosette of silky leaves cut into thread-like segments, then several reddish, wiry, much-branched stems with small thread leaves, the upper half a long narrow panicle of tiny yellow-green nodding heads. The model is round grey plates on the ground under bare straight wires with a dust of specks in the air beside them.

Artemisia frigida.note: A low silver-white mat of soft, finely cut, feathery leaves, with many upright leafy stems carrying nodding yellow button heads along their upper half: a soft silvery plume. The model is flat olive-grey round plates and a few bare wires. Nothing silver, nothing feathery.

Artemisia ludoviciana.note: Patches of upright stems, silver-white all over, with lance leaves 3 to 8 cm, some lobed, ending in a narrow leafy spike of small nodding grey-yellow buttons. The model has the silver and the upright leafy stems, which is most of it. The leaves are long stiff blades, and with no flower recorded the stems end in a leaf.

Asclepias ovalifolia.note: One or a few unbranched stems, knee high, with 4 to 6 pairs of oval grey-green leaves 5 to 8 cm, and one to three round clusters of cream flowers near the top; narrow upright pods. Recorded with 15 cm leaves on a 50 cm plant, so the model is a pagoda of huge plates with white specks lying on top.

Astragalus canadensis.note: A stout bushy plant to a metre with large pinnate leaves of 15 to 35 leaflets, and dense upright spikes 5 to 15 cm long of creamy to greenish-yellow nodding pea flowers; the brown pod spikes stand through winter. The model is a few thin stems with tiny leaves and a thin scatter of pale flecks.

Astragalus laxmannii.note: A low spreading clump of many stems with grey-green pinnate leaves, each stem ending in a dense egg-shaped head of purple and white pea flowers 2 to 3 cm across, like a clover. The model is one stem with a few tiny dark flecks scattered through the leaves: the dense purple heads are the plant.

Betula occidentalis.note: A clump of several stems with shiny coppery-red bark, twiggy and leafy from low down, small toothed oval leaves. The bark colour is right. The model is a fan of straight rods bare for most of their height under a flat cap of leaves, like a parasol.

Betula papyrifera.note: White peeling bark, an oval open crown of many fine branches and drooping twigs. The model is a white pole with four upright leaders and a thin scatter of leaves on each; leafless in April it has almost no branches at all. The bark is right, the crown is not a crown.

Blitum capitatum.note: A leafy, branching stem with triangular to arrowhead-shaped, coarsely toothed leaves, and round, bright red, strawberry-like clusters 1 to 1.5 cm across strung along the upper stem, which is the whole of what it is known by. The model is a stack of plain oval plates with no red anywhere: no flower or fruit shape is recorded.

Bouteloua gracilis.note: A low mat of fine, curling, grey-green blades a hand high, with thin stalks to 30 cm each carrying one to three combs: a one-sided spike 2 to 5 cm long, purple then straw, held out sideways like an eyelash and curling as it dries. The seed head is recorded correctly; the model shows only two or three small pale chips. The blades are wide straps, dark olive, and the plant is drawn as tall as its stalks.

Bromus ciliatus.note: A loose tuft of broad flat leaves, with a few tall stems each ending in an open, drooping panicle of large, flattened, hanging spikelets 1.5 to 2.5 cm long with short awns, like oats. The model shows a couple of specks at the top of a narrow column of straps: the hanging oat-like spikelets are the plant.

Calamagrostis canadensis.note: A big arching tussock of long, flat, drooping leaves, with stems to 1.5 m ending in a nodding, feathery, loosely branched plume 10 to 20 cm long, purplish then tan, that stands through winter. It is recorded as a contracted spike; it is an open nodding plume. The model's fan of stiff wide straps with two pale blocks at the top reads as a yucca more than a grass.

Calla palustris.note: Glossy heart-shaped leaves on long stalks from a creeping stem in shallow water; one white hood (a spathe) 4 to 6 cm behind a short knobby yellow-green club; then a tight club of red berries. The model's leaves on stalks are right. Its flower is a column of forty grey-white plates: it should be one white hood and one club.

Caltha natans.note: Round to kidney-shaped leaves 2 to 5 cm floating on the water or lying on mud, from trailing stems, with small white flowers 1 cm across of five petals round a green-yellow centre held just above them. The model does the job: floating notched leaves on water with white flowers. The flowers are too many and too big, all in one bunch.

Caltha palustris.note: A mound of glossy round to kidney-shaped leaves held up on thick hollow stalks, with shining deep yellow flowers 3 to 4 cm just above them, many at once. The model reads as a marsh marigold from above. Its leaves lie flat on the ground and are near black, and the flowers are pale straw with dark brown backs.

Campanula rotundifolia.note: Thin wiry stems with a few thread-narrow leaves, each carrying one to a few nodding violet-blue bells 2 cm long; the round leaves it is named for are small and at the base. The model is a dense tuft of broad grass blades under a cloud of thirty flat blue stars, half of them navy: a different plant.

Canadanthus modestus.note: Leafy stems with clasping lance leaves, branching at the top into purple daisies 3 to 4 cm across with many narrow rays, a sticky purplish cup beneath. The model is a few thin stems with grass-like leaves and a handful of tan specks: no purple anywhere.

Carex utriculata.note: Stands of stout stems with wide yellow-green leaves, each stem with thin male spikes at the top and below them two to four thick, dense cylinders 4 to 10 cm long, straw-yellow to orange-brown, of inflated beaked sacs. No seed head is recorded, so the model draws yellow daisy shapes lying flat in a ring round a dark column.

Cerastium arvense.note: A loose mat of slender stems with pairs of small narrow grey-green leaves 1 to 2 cm, covered in white flowers 1.5 cm across, five petals each notched halfway, on thin stalks above the leaves. The model reads as a low plant with white flowers on top, close in kind. The leaves are long stiff blades and there are far fewer flowers than a plant in bloom carries.

Chamaenerion angustifolium.note: A tall unbranched stem crowded with willow-like leaves, ending in a long tapering spike of magenta four-petalled flowers 2 to 3 cm, buds drooping at the tip, long red seed pods below that split into white fluff. The model's leafy stems are right in kind. Its flowers are pale pink and dark maroon squares floating round the stem, where the plant is a solid magenta spire.

Cinna latifolia.note: A loose woodland grass with broad, flat, soft, bright green leaves spaced up the stem, and a large, open, drooping panicle 15 to 30 cm long whose fine branches hang to one side. The seed head is recorded nodding; the model shows almost none. The body is the same stiff column of dark straps as every grass.

Cirsium flodmanii.note: A leafy thistle to a metre, the stem and leaf undersides white-woolly, the leaves deeply cut and spiny; each branch ends in a pink-purple brush 3 to 4 cm across on a spiny green urn. The model is a dark rosette of broad leaves under bare wires tipped with pink dots: not a thistle.

Clematis occidentalis.note: A slender woody vine with leaves of three pointed, heart-based leaflets 4 to 8 cm; nodding blue-violet lanterns of four long pointed sepals 4 to 6 cm; then silky feather-ball seed heads that last into winter. The model's vine is a few threads of tiny ladder leaves on the dogwood's side with flowers as specks in the air: the dogwood is all one sees. The sheet's camera frames the host, which makes a vine hard to judge.

Comandra umbellata.note: Patches of slender upright stems a hand high, with small, pale blue-green, oblong leaves up the stem, and clusters of small white to pinkish star flowers at the top. The model's white flowers at the top are right. The body is a spiky ball of long bright green blades, like a small yucca; the leaf surface is recorded glaucous and the colour does not follow it.

Comarum palustre.note: Sprawling reddish stems in wet ground; blue-green leaves of 5 to 7 toothed, oblong leaflets, the upper ones set like fingers; flowers 2 cm, a star of five pointed wine-red sepals round a dark red centre. It is recorded orange-red; every photograph is deep wine red. The model's cloud of orange and near-black flecks hovers above an upright ladder-leaf stem.

Coreopsis tinctoria.note: A slender, much-branched plant with leaves cut into thread-like segments, and many heads 3 to 4 cm: eight broad, notched yellow rays, each with a maroon base, round a dark red-brown button. The model is a thin leafy stem with a few small dark discs lying flat, the yellow rays hardly showing.

Cornus canadensis.note: A carpet of separate upright stems a hand high, each ending in one whorl of 4 to 6 pointed oval leaves with curved veins, and above it one flower of four broad white bracts 2 to 3 cm across round a green button; then a tight bunch of bright red berries in the centre of each whorl. The model is one mound of stacked plates with a pile of white confetti on top; its red berry bunches are close.

Cornus sericea.note: Many slender bright red stems, opposite oval leaves with curved veins, flat white clusters 4 to 5 cm across at the branch tips, white berries. The model has the red, on trunks as thick as an arm; the leaves are big plates in tiers; the flowers are specks floating above the shrub, and the berries do not show.

Corylus cornuta.note: A dense many-stemmed shrub of slender stems; bright green oval leaves, doubly toothed, 5 to 10 cm; hanging yellow catkins on bare twigs in April; nuts in a long-beaked bristly husk. The model is thick sticks carrying big leaf plates in tiers, and bare sticks in April.

Crataegus chrysocarpa.note: A dense, thorny, twiggy small tree; broad roundish leaves, sharply toothed and shallowly lobed; clusters of white five-petalled flowers in May; red haws. The model is a few thick forked trunks with leaf cards at the ends, no flower in May and no haws in August.

Cypripedium parviflorum.note: One stem with 3 to 5 pleated, strongly veined leaves that sheathe it and point up, and at the top one flower: a yellow pouch 3 to 5 cm with twisted maroon-brown ribbons either side. The model is a pagoda of dozens of leaf plates with small flat yellow discs lying on top.

Dalea purpurea.note: Several slender stems with leaves of 3 to 5 thread-narrow leaflets, each stem ending in a dense thimble 1 to 5 cm long and 1 cm thick: a ring of bright magenta flowers with orange anthers climbing a grey cone. The model's slender stems and small leaves are right. Its flowers are long open strings of dark violet dots, where the plant's is one solid thimble a stem.

Dasiphora fruticosa.note: A dense, rounded, fine-textured bush; small grey-green leaves of five narrow leaflets; yellow five-petalled flowers 2 to 3 cm scattered over the whole bush all summer; shredding red-brown bark. The model has the yellow flowers at their size, all in a flat cap above a sparse V of sticks.

Doellingeria umbellata.note: Tall leafy stems, lance leaves 8 to 15 cm, topped by a broad flat-topped cluster 10 to 30 cm across of many small white daisies with 7 to 14 rays and yellow centres. The model's leafy stems are right in kind; in August, mid-flowering, it shows no flowers at all.

Drosera rotundifolia.note: A rosette 3 to 8 cm across of round leaves on flat stalks, red and fringed with sticky glistening hairs, flat on the moss; one thin stalk with a few small white flowers down one side. The model is a few hair-thin lines: no rosette, no red. A plant this small may be beyond what a yard view can show, but a red rosette is drawable.

Drymocallis arguta.note: Stiff, upright, sticky-hairy stems from a tuft of basal leaves; leaves of 7 to 11 toothed leaflets; a tight flat cluster at the top of cream to pale yellow flowers 1.5 cm. The model's upright stems and top cluster are right in kind; the cluster is a flat cloud of yellow and near-black flecks, and the leaflets are plain ovals.

Elaeagnus commutata.note: Upright stems with brown scurfy twigs, silver leaves on both sides, small yellow flowers tucked in the leaf axils in June, silvery mealy berries that stay into winter. The model has the silver. It is a sparse V of brown trunks, and since no flower shape is recorded it never flowers; its berries do not show.

Elymus canadensis.note: A loose tuft of broad blue-green leaves, with stems to 1.2 m each ending in a thick, bristly spike 10 to 25 cm long that arches over and nods, its long awns curving outward, like a bearded rye. The model is a narrow dark column of stiff straps with one small pale upright block: the big nodding bristly head is the plant's whole character.

Equisetum arvense.note: Bright green jointed stems with whorls of slender green branches at every joint, the branches angled upward and often branching again, so the plant is a soft bottle-brush; in spring, separate pale brown stems with a cone. The model reads as a horsetail at once. The real plant's branches are longer, finer and more crowded, and its stems thinner.

Equisetum fluviatile.note: Stands of tall, smooth, hollow, bright green stems in shallow water, many with no branches at all and others with short irregular whorls in the middle; a dark cone at the tip of some. The model does the job: thin jointed stems with whorls in the middle. It is darker than the plant's light green.

Erigeron glabellus.note: A tuft of narrow spoon leaves, a few smaller leaves up each stem, and one to three daisies per stem, 2 to 3 cm, with a hundred or more narrow lilac, pink or white rays round a yellow centre. The model's heads face straight up, so from the side they are specks in the air above bare wires.

Erigeron philadelphicus.note: A rosette of soft spoon-shaped leaves and a hairy stem with clasping leaves, branching at the top into ten to thirty daisies 1.5 to 2.5 cm: a hundred or more thread-thin white to pale pink rays round a yellow centre. The model has the rosette, then bare wires and a few orange-brown specks in the air.

Eurybia conspicua.note: Large, rough, toothed oval leaves mostly on the lower stem, and an open flat-topped cluster above them of violet daisies 3 to 4 cm with yellow centres. The model is a solid cone of leaf plates to the top, like a pine cone, with a few specks.

Eurybia sibirica.note: A low spreading plant of leafy stems, lance to oval leaves 3 to 6 cm, each stem ending in one to a few lilac daisies 3 cm across with yellow centres. Recorded with 12 cm leaves on a 40 cm plant, so the model is a pagoda of leaf plates each a third of the plant wide, with a few specks on top.

Euthamia graminifolia.note: A bushy plant branching in its upper half, with many narrow grass-like leaves 4 to 8 cm, each branch ending in a small dense cluster of yellow so the top is one broad flat plate of gold. The model has the narrow leaves, drawn large and stiff; its flat top is a faint line of specks.

Eutrochium maculatum.note: A stout purple or purple-spotted stem to 1.5 m with whorls of 4 or 5 toothed lance leaves, topped by a broad, flat to domed head 10 to 20 cm across of fuzzy pink-purple. The model's whorled leaves up a tall stem are the right kind, the best whorled body so far; in August it shows no flower at all, and the leaves are thin blades.

Festuca hallii.note: A large dense tussock of stiff, rough, grey-green rolled leaves 20 to 30 cm long, with stems to 60 cm carrying narrow panicles of purplish spikelets. The model is the dark column of wide straps with tan blocks. Only four photographs and none of a whole tussock, so the body cannot be judged from the sheet.

Festuca saximontana.note: A small dense cushion of hair-fine, blue-grey leaves 5 to 10 cm tall, with many thin stems to 30 cm carrying narrow panicles 3 to 8 cm long, purplish then straw. The model's tuft with heads above it is right in kind; its leaves are wide flat straps and its heads are fat tan blocks. Six photographs.

Fragaria vesca.note: As Wild Strawberry, with thinner, brighter green, strongly veined leaflets whose end tooth is longer than its neighbours, and a pointed berry held above the leaves with its seeds on the surface. The model is the same as Wild Strawberry's, which is fair: little that is recorded tells them apart.

Fragaria virginiana.note: Tufts of long-stalked leaves, each of three broad, coarsely toothed, blue-green leaflets, joined by red runners; white five-petalled flowers 1.5 to 2 cm with a yellow centre, held about level with the leaves; small red strawberries hanging below. The model reads as a strawberry in flower. The leaflets are narrow rather than broad and toothed, and the berries sit out at the edge of the plant.

Gaillardia aristata.note: A clump of leafy stems, grey-green and hairy, the leaves running up the lower stem; heads 5 to 7 cm with yellow rays, red at the base, three-toothed at the tip, round a red-brown dome; a round seed ball after. The model is a flat near-black rosette with bare wire stalks and dark red discs hovering above their tips: the rays read dark orange, not yellow.

Galium boreale.note: A dense patch of many upright square stems, each ringed every few centimetres with a whorl of four narrow three-veined leaves 2 to 4 cm, topped with frothy pyramids of tiny white flowers. It is recorded sprawling; it stands up. The model is a ring of specks on the ground, three bare hairs and a ball of dots in the air.

Galium triflorum.note: Weak trailing stems with whorls of six bright green leaves, widest above the middle and tipped with a point, like spokes of a wheel, spaced along the stem; tiny greenish-white flowers in threes; small bristly burs. The model is a dense starburst of long blades from one point with white specks: none of the neat spaced wheels of six.

Gentianella amarella.note: A small stiff plant with opposite lance leaves, and narrow upright tubes 1 to 2 cm long that open into 4 or 5 small pointed lobes, lilac to violet, bunched in the leaf axils all the way up the stem. It is recorded pink and 2 cm across. The model is a tuft of long blades under large flat pink and near-black plates.

Geranium richardsonii.note: An open bushy plant of long-stalked leaves cut into 5 to 7 sharp-toothed fingers, red in autumn; white flowers 2.5 to 3 cm with five rounded petals lined in purple, in pairs above the leaves. The model's white flowers are the right size and read well; the leaves are plain ovals in a stack, and the flowers bunch in one cloud at the top.

Geum aleppicum.note: A leafy, hairy, branching stem to a metre; leaves of sharply toothed leaflets with a large wedge-shaped end one; yellow five-petalled flowers 1.5 to 2 cm at the branch tips; round bristly bur heads. The model is a small ladder-leaf rosette under a bundle of bare wires with a thin scatter of flowers above.

Geum macrophyllum.note: Basal leaves with a very large round, lobed end leaflet and a few small ones below it; leafy branching stems with three-lobed leaves; yellow five-petalled flowers 1.5 cm; round bur heads of hooked seeds. The model's leaves are ladders of small equal leaflets, near black; the stalks are bare wires and the flowers a pale cloud above them.

Geum rivale.note: Nodding bells on arching hairy stalks: a dusky purple-maroon cup round cream to pink petals; basal leaves with a big rounded end leaflet; bristly seed heads. The model is one tall stalk under a flat cloud of pale lilac and black stars, with ladder leaves.

Geum triflorum.note: A rosette of ferny leaves, many toothed leaflets growing larger toward the tip; several reddish stalks each with three nodding, closed, dusky rose-pink urns; then long feathery pink plumes, the smoke it is named for. The model's rosette is the right kind. It has one stalk, open stars facing sideways, and no plumes.

Glyceria grandis.note: A stout wetland grass with broad flat leaves, topped by a very large, open, much-branched panicle 20 to 40 cm long and nearly as wide, its many small spikelets purple, nodding at the ends of fine branches. The seed head is recorded correctly as an open panicle; the model shows a faint speck at the top of a narrow column of straps.

Glyceria striata.note: A slender wetland grass in loose tufts, with an open panicle 10 to 20 cm long of drooping thread-fine branches beaded with small oval spikelets, green then purple. The model's pale beaded heads are the right idea and the best seed head of the grasses so far; they stand stiffly upright where the plant's droop, on the same column of wide straps.

Glycyrrhiza lepidota.note: A bushy plant with leaves of 11 to 19 lance leaflets; dense upright spikes of cream pea flowers, shorter than the leaves; then clusters of rust-brown burs covered in hooked prickles that stay on the dead stems all winter. The model's ladder leaves are right. It is one stem with pale dots scattered round its top, and no burs.

Grindelia squarrosa.note: A rounded bushy plant, much branched, with small toothed oblong leaves and dozens of bright yellow daisies 2.5 to 3.5 cm, each on a green bur of curled-back sticky bracts. The model is a few thin stems with long grass blades and five or six small orange specks.

Hedysarum americanum.note: A bushy clump of leafy stems, leaves of 9 to 21 leaflets, each stem ending in a long, slim, one-sided raceme of drooping pink-purple pea flowers; flat pods pinched into round links. The model's pinnate leaves read well. It is one stem, and its flowers are a cloud of pink flecks spread across the whole plant, not on spikes.

Hedysarum boreale.note: A bushy clump of many stems with grey-green leaves of 9 to 15 narrow leaflets; racemes of bright magenta to red-purple pea flowers 1.5 to 2 cm; pods of flat round joints. It is recorded pale pink. The model is one stem of ladder leaves with pale pink flecks scattered round it.

Helenium autumnale.note: Leafy winged stems branching at the top into many heads 3 to 5 cm: wedge-shaped yellow rays with three teeth, bent back round a yellow to green-yellow ball 1 to 2 cm across. The centre is recorded brown; it is yellow. The model in September is an olive-brown stem with a few tiny dark discs.

Helianthus nuttallii.note: Tall slender stems to 2 m, narrow lance leaves 8 to 15 cm, several sunflowers 5 to 8 cm with yellow rays round a yellow-brown centre. The model's tall leafy stems are right in kind; its leaves are broad paddles, and the heads are small dark discs in the air above the plant with no yellow showing.

Helianthus pauciflorus.note: Slender stiff stems, few and rough lance leaves mostly on the lower half, the upper stem nearly bare, each ending in a sunflower 6 to 8 cm with yellow rays round a dark red-brown disc. The model is a dense column of huge overlapping leaves, like a tobacco plant, with small dark heads buried in it.

Hesperostipa comata.note: A dense bunch of fine, rolled, grey-green leaves, with stems whose seeds each trail a thread-thin awn 10 to 15 cm long, straight then curling and tangling, so the heads shimmer silver in wind. The model's bristly head is a flat fan of rays on a stick, like a dandelion clock, beside a spray of wide dark straps.

Hesperostipa spartea.note: A tall bunchgrass with long narrow leaves and nodding stems whose few large seeds each carry a stout awn 12 to 20 cm long, twisted below and bent twice, hanging like quills. The model draws the same flat dandelion-clock fans as Needle and Thread.

Heterotheca villosa.note: A low grey-hairy clump of many leafy stems, small oblong grey-green leaves 2 to 4 cm, and many bright yellow daisies 2 to 3 cm. The model is tall thin stems with long green grass blades; its heads are small and dark from the side.

Heuchera richardsonii.note: A rosette of round, scalloped, shallowly lobed leaves and a few tall bare hairy stalks, each ending in a narrow spike of small greenish-yellow to tan bells. The model's rosette and bare stalks are the right kind. Its flowers are red stars scattered in a cloud off the stalks: every photograph shows green-yellow, and they sit on the stalk.

Hieracium umbellatum.note: A leafy stem, narrow toothed lance leaves crowded all the way up and no rosette at flowering, branching at the top into a loose cluster of yellow dandelion-like heads 2 to 3 cm; a tan pappus ball after. The model is a hand-sized rosette under bare wires with a few yellow specks: nothing of the plant.

Hippuris vulgaris.note: Unbranched stems standing out of shallow water, closely ringed with whorls of 6 to 12 soft, narrow leaves 1 to 3 cm that curve upward, so each stem is a soft green bottle-brush tapering to the tip; yellow-green. The model reads as the plant: whorled upright stems. Its whorls are short stiff spikes set far apart on a thick dark stem, more like a bamboo cane.

Juniperus communis.note: A dense evergreen mat or low spreading bush of sharp awl needles in threes, bright green with a white stripe, with blue-black berries. The model is bare brown sticks radiating from a point with dark slivers on them: a dead bush. Nothing of the green mass that is the whole plant.

Juniperus horizontalis.note: A flat evergreen carpet of long trailing woody branches with feathery sprays of tiny scale leaves, blue-green to grey-green, purplish in winter, with blue-white berries. The model is a star of grass-like blades from one point, bright green: a tuft, not a woody mat. Only six photographs, none in flower since it has none.

Koeleria macrantha.note: A small dense tuft of short, narrow, grey-green basal leaves a hand high, with many stiff bare stems to 50 cm each ending in a dense, narrow, silvery-green to pale gold spike 4 to 10 cm long that opens fluffy in flower. No seed head is recorded, so the model draws white daisies lying flat above a spray of long wide straps as tall as the stems.

Larix laricina.note: An open, airy cone of slender level branches carrying soft tufts of light green needles; bare and twiggy in winter. The model's colour is right, but the crown is solid flat plates with the spruce's pencil tip: nothing of the tree's feathery, see-through look.

Lathyrus ochroleucus.note: A climbing pea with leaves of 3 to 5 pairs of broad oval blue-green leaflets ending in a tendril, large leafy stipules, and one-sided racemes of 5 to 10 creamy yellow-white pea flowers 1.5 cm. The model's vine is a wisp of tiny leaves at the dogwood's foot with grey specks above the host.

Lathyrus venosus.note: A stout climbing pea with leaves of 4 to 6 pairs of oval, veined leaflets ending in a tendril, and dense one-sided racemes of 10 to 20 purple and pink pea flowers. The model's vine is a wisp at the dogwood's foot with flecks in the air above the host.

Ledum groenlandicum.note: A low evergreen shrub; narrow leathery leaves with rolled edges, rusty wool beneath, drooping in winter; round white clusters 4 to 5 cm across at the shoot tips. The model's leaves are broad bright plates on a thick trunk and its flowers are white specks hovering above the bush.

Lemna trisulca.note: Thin, translucent, olive-green fronds 0.5 to 1 cm long, pointed and stalked, joined crosswise in chains and tangled mats that float just under the surface, not on it. The model is round green dots on the water, the common duckweed's look. At this size the difference hardly shows in a yard. Only four photographs.

Leymus innovatus.note: A stiff blue-green grass with rolled leaves and a dense, erect to slightly arching spike 5 to 12 cm long, grey-purple and visibly hairy. The model's pale upright blocks are the right position; they are flat tan rectangles, and the leaves are wide straps. Only six photographs, none of the whole plant in leaf.

Liatris ligulistylis.note: An unbranched stem with narrow leaves that shrink upward, carrying a few to a dozen round shaggy button heads 2 to 3 cm across, vivid purple-magenta, well spaced, the top one largest and first to open; dark red-purple bracts. The model's leafy stem is right in kind; its heads are pale pink dots a few millimetres across. Recorded 1.4 cm and pink.

Lilium philadelphicum.note: One straight stem with narrow leaves scattered up it and a whorl of them just under the flower; one to three upright, open cups 6 to 8 cm across, six orange-red tepals narrowed to stalks at the base, yellow and purple-spotted inside. The model is a grass tussock with orange and brown stars floating over it. The flower's size and count are right; it is on the wrong body and too orange, with no spotted throat.

Linnaea borealis.note: Thin trailing stems with pairs of small, round, glossy evergreen leaves 1 to 2 cm, and thread-like stalks a finger high that fork at the top to hang two pink bells side by side. The model is a mound of large plates with four pink specks on it: no upright forked stalks, which are the plant's name.

Linum lewisii.note: A tuft of many wiry stems, closely set with tiny narrow leaves, arching at the top with sky-blue flowers 2.5 to 3 cm: five broad petals with darker veins and a yellow eye; round seed capsules on curved stalks. One of the better models: thin leafy stems and pale blue flowers at the top. Half the flowers render near-black navy, and it has three stems where the plant has dozens.

Lonicera dioica.note: A twining woody vine with opposite, oval, blue-green leaves, whitish beneath; the top pair below each flower cluster is joined into one disc round the stem, which stays on the vine all winter as a papery cup. The flowers are a bunch of yellow to orange-red tubes with long stamens in that cup; then red berries in it. The model's vine is two hanging chains of small leaves with specks in the air.

Lonicera involucrata.note: An upright shrub with large pointed opposite leaves; pairs of yellow tubular flowers in the leaf axils, cupped in green bracts that turn dark red around a pair of shiny black berries. The catalogue has the flower red and the fruit red: the red is the bracts, the flowers are yellow and the berries black. The model's flowers are specks floating outside the bush.

Lysimachia ciliata.note: Upright stems with opposite, broad, pointed oval leaves on fringed stalks; yellow five-petalled flowers 2 cm, each petal ending in a small point, nodding singly on long stalks from the upper leaf axils. It is recorded as a raceme. The model has thin grass-blade leaves and a column of orange and brown flecks round the stem top.

Maianthemum amplexicaule.note: One arching, zigzag stem with 6 to 12 broad, pointed, pleated leaves in two flat rows, like a ladder, ending in a creamy plume 5 to 12 cm; then a bunch of red speckled berries at the stem tip. The model is a spiral pagoda of plates round a straight pole, the flowers a few specks to one side, the berries scattered in the air.

Maianthemum canadense.note: A carpet of separate small stems, each with one to three glossy heart-based oval leaves and, on flowering stems, one short dense spike of tiny white four-part stars standing above them; berries speckled, then red. The model is one big stack of plates with white stars scattered in its centre and red balls on top.

Maianthemum stellatum.note: One arching, unbranched stem with narrow lance leaves in two flat rows, folded along the midrib and clasping the stem, ending in a short raceme of 5 to 10 white six-pointed stars; berries green with dark stripes, then dark red, at the stem tip. The model is a spiral pagoda of broad plates with no flower (none is recorded) and red dots through the stack.

Matteuccia struthiopteris.note: A vase of large fronds to 1.5 m, each a broad feather widest above the middle and tapering to the base, of 20 to 60 pairs of narrow, deeply cut leaflets set close together, bright green; fiddleheads in spring; short dark-brown fertile fronds that stand all winter. The model is a few thin wands with a dozen separate dark ovals each: it reads as a willow twig, not a fern.

Mentha canadensis.note: Square stems with opposite, toothed, pointed oval leaves, and at each upper leaf pair a dense ball of tiny pale lilac to pink flowers hugging the stem, the stem tip ending in leaves. The model's whorls are the right idea, set only at the top and dark violet. The body is a pagoda of leaf plates.

Menyanthes trifoliata.note: From a thick creeping stem in shallow water, long stalks each holding three broad, smooth, oval leaflets 4 to 8 cm above the surface, and a stout stalk with a dense club of white stars whose petals are thickly fringed with white hairs, pink in bud. The model is thick green posts with tiny leaves at the top and loose white stars beside them: the three big leaflets are the plant.

Mertensia paniculata.note: A loose leafy clump of arching stems with pointed oval, strongly veined leaves 5 to 12 cm, and at each stem's end a drooping bunch of blue bells 1 to 1.5 cm, pink in bud. The model is a solid cone of leaf plates with a cloud of dark specks beside its top: nothing nods, nothing is blue from a step away.

Mitella nuda.note: A few round, scalloped, hairy leaves on stalks, a few centimetres across, and a thread-thin bare stalk a hand high with a few green-yellow flowers whose petals are fringed like snowflakes. The model is a big mound of stacked angular plates with white specks in the middle: no round leaves, no stalk.

Monarda fistulosa.note: A leafy clump of square stems with opposite, toothed, lance to oval grey-green leaves; each stem ends in one round shaggy head 4 to 6 cm of pale lilac tubes; dark round seed heads stand all winter. The best body so far: leafy, upright, opposite. The heads are small clusters of pink and maroon balls rather than one lilac mop, and the leaves are thin as grass.

Muhlenbergia cuspidata.note: A dense tuft of wiry, thread-fine leaves from a knotty base, with very slender spike-like panicles a few millimetres wide; the whole clump turns orange-tan in autumn. The model's seed heads are tan blocks as wide as a hand, many times too thick, over wide dark straps. Seven photographs.

Myriophyllum sibiricum.note: Underwater stems with whorls of feather-like leaves cut into thread-fine segments, and thin reddish spikes standing a few centimetres out of the water with small flowers in whorls. The model is a scatter of broad oval leaves on the water, like a floating pondweed: the feathers are the plant.

Nassella viridula.note: A dense bunch of fine, rolled, bright green leaves, with stems to 80 cm ending in a narrow, upright, greenish-then-straw panicle 10 to 25 cm long with fine wavy awns. No seed head is recorded, so the model draws white daisy shapes lying flat beside a column of wide straps.

Nuphar variegata.note: Large oval floating leaves 10 to 25 cm with a deep narrow notch, crowded on the water, and yellow globes 4 to 5 cm across held just above it on thick stalks: five or six thick cupped sepals, red inside at the base, round a flat yellow disc. The model's notched pads on water read as a pond-lily. Its flowers are small flat yellow stars lying on the pads, where the plant's is a ball on a stalk.

Oenothera biennis.note: A flat rosette the first year; the second, a stout leafy stalk to 1.5 m, lance leaves all the way up, ending in a spike of four-petalled yellow flowers 3 to 5 cm that opens from the bottom; woody seed capsules stand through winter. The model is a hand-sized rosette under 1.5 m bare wires: the tall leafy stalk, which is the plant, is missing.

Oenothera suffrutescens.note: A knee-high bunch of slender leafy stems, the leaves small, narrow and grey-green; a wand of flowers about 1 cm across with four white petals, turned to one side, that age pink then red, and long stamens. It is recorded with a 5 cm flower (the evening primrose's) and a 12 cm basal leaf: the model is a rosette under a club of huge red stars.

Opuntia fragilis.note: A low, tight, tangled mat of small plump joints, nearly as thick as wide, grey-green to purplish and hidden under long pale spines; pale yellow flowers 4 to 5 cm, often flushed orange or red, with red stamen stalks. The model's chains of spiny pads with yellow flowers read as a prickly-pear. The pads are scattered far apart, flat and bright green, where the plant is one dense spiny cushion.

Orthocarpus luteus.note: A small stiff plant, one or a few upright stems crowded with narrow leaves, the upper half a dense leafy spike with golden-yellow club-shaped flowers poking out of green bracts. The model is close: narrow-leaved stems with yellow flowers up the spike. Some flowers render dark orange-brown and the leaves are long.

Osmorhiza longistylis.note: A leafy woodland plant: large leaves divided two or three times into broad, toothed leaflets, on the stem as well as at the base, and small open umbels of white flowers just above the leaves. The model is five tall bare wires from a few small ladder leaves, the umbels grey flecks off to one side in the air.

Oxytropis campestris.note: A tuft of silky grey-green leaves with many small leaflets, and several bare stalks each ending in a dense head of pale yellow to cream pea flowers. Its name says yellow and most of the photographs are cream; it is recorded purple (photographs 1, 3 and 13 are a purple locoweed, likely another species). The model is one stalk with purple specks scattered around it in the air.

Penstemon gracilis.note: A slender plant: one to a few thin stems from a small rosette, pairs of narrow leaves, and a narrow open raceme of pale lilac tubes 1.5 to 2 cm, held level, with a white, purple-lined throat. The model has the tubes on the stems, the right idea, but dark violet and stubby, on a dense bush of broad blades.

Penstemon procerus.note: A low mat of small lance leaves and slender stems carrying one to several tight, ball-like whorls of small deep blue-purple tubes 1 cm long. Recorded with the genus's 2.5 cm flower and 8 cm leaf. The model's blue-purple tubes on stems are right in kind and colour; the body is a spiky rosette of long blades, like a yucca.

Persicaria amphibia.note: In water, glossy oblong leaves floating flat and pink clubs standing above them; on land, a leafy stem with broad lance leaves. Either way the flower is a dense, solid, bright pink egg or cylinder 2 to 4 cm tall, one at each stem tip. The model is a star of stiff blades with thin strings of dots too small to see.

Petasites frigidus.note: In April and May a thick, scaly stalk comes up before the leaves, topped with a bunch of white to pinkish heads. The leaves follow: large, cut into 5 to 7 toothed lobes like a hand, green above and white-woolly beneath, held up on long stalks. The model in April is a near-black lobed rosette flat on the ground with a few wires, and no flower, since none is recorded.

Physostegia ledinghamii.note: Square stems with opposite, toothed lance leaves, ending in a spike of pink-purple tubular two-lipped flowers 1.5 to 2.5 cm in four rows. The model is a tower of long blades with dark purple specks hidden among them. Only four photographs.

Picea glauca.note: A dense cone, branches to the ground when grown in the open, blue-green. The model reads as a spruce; the flat stacked plates and the smooth pencil tip are the giveaway, and the lowest branches stop well above the ground.

Picea mariana.note: A very narrow spire with short drooping branches and often a dense club at the top. The model is White Spruce's: flat stacked plates with a smooth solid cone for a tip. It reads as a spruce from a distance; the plates and the pencil-point tip are what give it away.

Pinus banksiana.note: Open irregular crown of long limbs carrying yellow-green needle tufts, curved cones held along the branches. The model is a pole with small dark whorls, a bottle brush: too narrow, too little foliage, and darker than the yellow-green in every photograph.

Polygala senega.note: A clump of several unbranched stems with small lance leaves, each stem ending in a dense, tapering, white spike 2 to 4 cm long, like a small white cone. The model's clump of leafy stems is the right kind; no flower is recorded, so the white spikes that are the plant in June are missing, and the leaves are long blades.

Populus balsamifera.note: Tall straight bole, grey furrowed bark, an open irregular crown of ascending limbs. The model is a narrow tuft on a long square-sectioned post: the crown is too small for the trunk and the trunk reads as a fence post at the base.

Populus tremuloides.note: A pale smooth trunk with black scars and a rounded crown of fine branches in the top third to half, the round leaves on flat stalks. The model is a very long pole with a dozen leaf clumps near the top and, leafless, almost no branches. Bark colour is right.

Potentilla anserina.note: Rosettes of feather-like leaves of many sharply toothed leaflets, green above and silver-white silky beneath, joined by long red runners; bright yellow flowers 2 cm across, one to a stalk, scattered among the leaves. One of the better mats: the pinnate leaves and the yellow read at once. The flowers are piled in one clump in the centre, and nothing shows the silver undersides or the runners.

Potentilla gracilis.note: A tuft of long-stalked leaves, each a hand of 5 to 7 toothed fingers, green above and white-woolly beneath; slender stems with an open cluster of bright yellow flowers 1.5 to 2 cm, petals notched. It is recorded pinnate; the leaf is palmate. The model's posture is close; its flower cloud is half near-black flecks.

Primula pauciflora.note: A small rosette of smooth, upright, light green spoon leaves and one or a few bare stalks, each with a spray of nodding magenta darts: petals swept straight back, a yellow and white ring, a dark point. The model's rosette, stalk and cluster are the right kind. The flowers are flat pale pink stars beside the stalk, and the rosette is near black.

Prosartes trachycarpa.note: A forking, branching stem with broad, pointed, parallel-veined oval leaves held flat in two rows; one or two creamy bells hang from each branch tip under the leaves; then round, rough-skinned berries, orange to red. The model's broad oval leaves on upright stems read well. No flower is recorded for it, so it never flowers or fruits, and the stems do not fork.

Prunus pensylvanica.note: Slender tree, shiny red-brown bark with horizontal lenticels, drooping lance leaves 8 cm, flat clusters of 5 to 7 white flowers in May, red cherries on long stalks. The model's leaf cards are long stiff blades pointing every way, so it reads as a palm or a yucca; no flower shows in May and no fruit in August.

Prunus virginiana.note: A tall dense shrub; oval leaves, widest above the middle, finely toothed; white bottlebrush racemes 8 to 10 cm long all over it in May; hanging racemes of dark red to black cherries. The model is a bundle of thick grey sticks with sparse leaf cards at the tips, with no flower in May and no fruit in August: none of what makes a chokecherry.

Pulsatilla nuttalliana.note: The flowers come before the leaves: a tuft of furry stalks, each with one cup of six pale lavender to white sepals round a big yellow centre, 4 to 6 cm; then long feathery seed heads; the leaves, cut into many narrow fingers, grow after. The model is a 60 cm near-black rosette of broad lobed leaves under two flat purple stars.

Pyrola asarifolia.note: A small flat rosette of round, leathery, glossy dark leaves, and one bare reddish stalk a hand or two high carrying 8 to 20 nodding pink cups spaced up it, each with a long curved style. The model is a big spiky mound of long angular blades with pink stars in a flat cluster in the middle: the single upright stalk of bells is missing.

Ranunculus rhomboideus.note: A small plant, a hand high: a few long-stalked basal leaves, oval to diamond-shaped with a scalloped edge and no lobes, and stem leaves cut into narrow fingers; pale lemon flowers 1.5 to 2 cm with five narrow petals. The model is a large near-black rosette of lobed leaves, wider than the plant is tall, with its flowers in a cloud off to one side.

Ratibida columnifera.note: Slender branching stems with sparse grey-green leaves cut into narrow fingers; each long bare stalk ends in a column 2 to 4 cm tall, grey-green then dark brown, with 4 to 8 yellow rays hanging down from its base. The model is a pagoda of broad leaf plates with small flat heads lying among them: no column, which is the plant's name.

Ribes americanum.note: A leafy mound with maple-like lobed leaves dotted with gold glands beneath; drooping racemes of creamy yellow bell flowers; black berries. The model is a believable leafy mound. Its berries are red, and the catalogue records them red: they are black. In April its flowers are specks floating above bare sticks.

Ribes glandulosum.note: A low sprawling currant; maple-like leaves of 5 to 7 sharp lobes; upright racemes of small white-pink flowers; red bristly berries. The model is a low spreading bush with red berry strings, some hanging in the air beside it; the leaves are plain ovals.

Ribes hudsonianum.note: An upright shrub with large maple-like leaves of 3 to 5 lobes; upright racemes of small white flowers in May; black berries. The model is a believable leafy bush, the best of the shrubs so far; its leaves are unlobed plates, no flower shows in May, and some of its black berries hang outside the plant.

Ribes lacustre.note: A low sprawling shrub with bristly stems; glossy maple-like leaves cut into 3 to 5 lobes; drooping racemes of small pinkish saucer flowers; dark purple-black bristly berries. The model is bare sticks with a few small plain leaves; its berries are red and some hang in the air beside the plant; in May its flowers are a cloud above it.

Ribes oxyacanthoides.note: A low bristly, thorny shrub; small rounded leaves cut into 3 to 5 lobes; flowers singly or in twos and threes in the axils, greenish white; smooth berries ripening purple-black. It is recorded as a raceme of 12 and a red berry. The model's two bare elbowed canes reaching out sideways are the first thing the eye sees.

Ribes triste.note: A low sprawling currant of the forest floor; broad leaves of 3 to 5 shallow lobes; drooping racemes of small reddish-purple saucer flowers; strings of bright red, shiny currants. The model is a low leafy bush with red berry strings, close in kind. Its leaves are plain ovals and several of its berry strings hang in the air well outside the plant.

Rosa acicularis.note: Slender bristly stems; leaves of 5 to 7 oval toothed leaflets; pink flowers 5 to 7 cm across with a yellow centre, many open at once; red pear-shaped hips. The model's leaflets are narrow blades, so it reads as a willow; the flowers are a few specks, some dark; no hip shows in August.

Rosa arkansana.note: A low rose, knee high at most, dying back hard; leaves of 9 to 11 leaflets; pink flowers 4 to 5 cm in clusters at the stem tips; round red hips. The model reads as a low rose in flower, the flowers at their size. The base is a thick trunk, the leaflets are narrow, and no hip shows in September.

Rosa woodsii.note: A thicket of red-brown prickly stems; leaves of 5 to 9 oval toothed leaflets; pink flowers 4 to 5 cm, several together; clusters of red hips. The model is thick brown sticks with narrow-bladed leaves, a few pink specks floating above it and no hips.

Rubus arcticus.note: A hand-high plant in patches: leaves of three rounded, toothed leaflets, and one deep rose-magenta flower 2 to 2.5 cm per shoot, the petals narrow at the base; a red raspberry. The model is the Dewberry's tuft under a bouquet of pale pink: too many flowers, too pale, on narrow blades.

Rubus idaeus.note: Arching bristly canes forming a thicket as wide as it is tall; leaves of 3 to 5 broad toothed leaflets, pale beneath; white flowers with small narrow petals; red raspberries. The model is a narrow upright bundle of straight canes on one stem with narrow blades: the right height, none of the arching or the broad leaves.

Rubus pubescens.note: Long runners trailing over the forest floor with short upright shoots, each leaf of three broad, sharply toothed, pointed leaflets; one to three small white flowers with narrow upright petals; a dark red raspberry of a few large beads. The model is a tuft of narrow blades from one point under a big bouquet of white flowers: a different, showier plant.

Sagittaria cuneata.note: A tuft of long-stalked arrowhead leaves, the two back lobes long and pointed, and a stalk with whorls of three white flowers 2 to 2.5 cm, three round petals round a yellow centre. One of the best models: arrowhead leaves on stalks and flowers in whorls. Half the flowers render grey-black and the leaves are a dark teal where the plant is a light yellow-green.

Salix bebbiana.note: A big shrub or small tree of many crooked stems, bushy from low down; dull green elliptic leaves, pale beneath; yellow catkins on bare twigs in April. The model is three or four thick straight trunks with leaves only at the top, and in April it is bare sticks with no catkins.

Salix discolor.note: A tall many-stemmed willow, leafy to the ground; elliptic leaves, blue-white beneath; silvery furry catkins along bare twigs in March and April, which is the whole of what it is known for. The model is a narrow bundle of thick straight poles with leaves at the top, and in March it is bare sticks with no catkins.

Salix exigua.note: A thicket of slender wands thick with long, very narrow silvery grey-green leaves: a soft feathery grey mass. The model is a grey skeleton with slivers, which reads as dead or thorny. Many of the photographs are from the American south-west; the form is the same.

Salix interior.note: Thickets of slender upright wands on sandbars, each closely set with long narrow leaves, green to silvery; slim yellow catkins on leafy shoots. The model is three thick trunks with tufts of slivers: nothing of the dense leafy wand.

Salix petiolaris.note: A dense clump of slender stems thick with narrow lance leaves 5 to 10 cm long, green above and silvery beneath; catkins in April and May. The model is a grey skeleton with slivers for leaves: it reads as a dead bush. In April it has no catkins.

Schizachne purpurascens.note: A loose tuft of narrow leaves with slender stems ending in a sparse, drooping panicle of a few large purplish spikelets 2 cm long with spreading awns, hanging from hair-fine branches. The seed head is recorded nodding; the model shows faint pale flecks standing upright in a column of wide straps.

Schoenoplectus acutus.note: Round, smooth, leafless, grey-green stems to 2.5 m, as thick as a finger at the base and tapering to a point, in open stands; a drooping bunch of red-brown spikelets hangs from one side just below the stem's tip. The model is the cattail's column of flat blades with small orange plates floating beside it: it has no flat blades at all.

Scutellaria galericulata.note: A slender plant with opposite, short, scallop-edged lance leaves 2 to 5 cm, and blue-violet hooded flowers 1.5 to 2 cm in pairs in the leaf axils, both turned to one side. The model scatters its flowers through the plant, which is close to right. They are near-black violet, and the body is a dense bush of long stiff blades.

Shepherdia argentea.note: A thorny shrub, silvery on both sides of its narrow oblong leaves, pale grey twigs; tiny yellow flowers on bare twigs in May; masses of bright red berries along the branches. The model has the silver, which is most of the plant; the trunks are too thick and the berries do not show.

Shepherdia canadensis.note: A rounded leafy shrub; opposite oval leaves, dark green above, silvery with rust-brown dots beneath; brown scurfy twigs; red berries clustered tight at the nodes along the stems. The model is bare forked sticks with a few grey leaves, and its berries are red specks scattered through the air around it.

Sisyrinchium montanum.note: A small stiff tuft of flat, narrow, pale green iris-like blades, each flat stem carrying one or two blue-violet stars 1.5 to 2 cm with six pointed tepals and a yellow eye, held at the top beside a pointed bract; round seed capsules. The model reads as the plant: a tuft of blades with blue flowers at the top. It is too dense and dark, and half the flowers render navy.

Sium suave.note: A tall, hollow, ridged stem with leaves of 7 to 17 narrow, saw-toothed lance leaflets, topped by several domed white umbels 5 to 12 cm across. The model's ladder leaves up a tall stem are the right kind. Its umbels are small grey smudges where the plant's are broad white domes, and the leaves are dark teal.

Solidago altissima.note: A tall leafy stem, rough and grey-downy, under a broad pyramid of arching, one-sided branches solid with small yellow heads; grey-tan fluff after. The model is a few thin stems and a faint dust of dots, nothing yellow from two steps away.

Solidago gigantea.note: A tall, smooth, leafy stem topped by a large pyramid of bright yellow on arching, one-sided branches; the fluffy tan seed plumes stand into winter. The model is a few thin stems with small leaves and a faint dust of dots: nothing yellow from two steps away.

Solidago glutinosa.note: A small goldenrod: a tuft of spoon-shaped basal leaves and one unbranched stem ending in a narrow, dense, upright wand of yellow heads about 1 cm across. The model's yellow stars are visible, more than on the tall goldenrods; they are scattered round a star-shaped tower of long blades, not gathered in a wand.

Solidago lepida.note: A leafy stem with many toothed lance leaves, topped by a dense pyramid or plume of bright yellow, 10 to 20 cm tall, the branches often arching to one side. The model in August, its flowering, shows a dozen yellow specks among stiff blades: a goldenrod with no gold.

Solidago missouriensis.note: A low, smooth goldenrod: narrow three-veined lance leaves, larger at the base, and one compact bright yellow plume 5 to 15 cm, often nodding to one side. The model is a dense tuft of long stiff blades with a dozen small yellow stars lost among them.

Solidago rigida.note: A stout, hairy, grey-green plant with broad, stiff, oval leaves, large and long-stalked at the base and clasping up the stem, under a dense flat-topped head of large deep yellow flowers. It is recorded as a plume with lance leaves; it is the one goldenrod here with a flat top and oval leaves. The model is a thin stem with small leaves and a sparse spray of dots.

Sparganium eurycarpum.note: A clump of long, stiff, keeled, bright yellow-green leaves, with a zigzag branching stalk carrying round white pompoms of flowers that become green spiky burs 2 to 3 cm across, like small maces. The model is a dark tight column of blades with no flower in June and no burs: the round burs are how the plant is known.

Spiraea alba.note: Slender upright wands, closely set with small toothed lance leaves, each ending in a dense white steeple of tiny flowers 5 to 15 cm tall; the brown seed heads stand through winter. It is recorded as a flat-topped cluster; it is a cone (a panicle). The model is thick canes with long stiff blades and specks floating above.

Spiranthes romanzoffiana.note: A few narrow leaves at the base and one stem ending in a dense, thick, cream-white spike 5 to 10 cm tall, the hooded flowers packed in three spiralling rows. The model is a tall dense tuft of grass blades with small grey dots scattered loosely in the air above it.

Stachys pilosa.note: A hairy square stem with opposite, toothed, lance to oblong leaves, ending in a spike of separate whorls of pale pink-lilac two-lipped flowers, the lower lip spotted purple. The model's whorls spaced up the stem are the right idea. They are dark violet dots, where the plant is pale pink, and the leaves are thin grass blades.

Stuckenia pectinata.note: Dense underwater beds of thread-fine leaves on much-branched stems, all combed one way by the current, bright green to olive; small beaded spikes that barely reach the surface. The model shows a dozen short blades on the water, which is fair for a submerged plant seen from the bank; the plant is far denser and its leaves are threads.

Symphoricarpos albus.note: A fine twiggy shrub of slender arching stems; small roundish opposite leaves, dull blue-green; tiny pink bells; clusters of white berries that stay into winter and are how most people know it. The model's canes are thick, its flowers hover above it in the air, and the white berries do not show.

Symphoricarpos occidentalis.note: A dense colony of upright stems to a metre, oval grey-green leaves 3 to 6 cm, clusters of small pink-white flowers at the tips and in the axils, greenish-white berries that blacken over winter. The model is a pile of large bright plates, like a cabbage; no flower shows in July and no berry in September.

Symphyotrichum boreale.note: A very slender plant: one thin reddish stem with a few narrow, grass-like leaves, and a few white to pale lilac daisies 1.5 to 2 cm at the top. The model is a dense column of broad stiff blades, like a yucca, with tan specks above it.

Symphyotrichum ciliolatum.note: Heart-shaped lower leaves on winged stalks, smaller lance leaves up the stem, and an open cluster of pale blue-violet daisies 2 to 3 cm with 12 to 25 rays. The model is the same thin stem and grass blades as Smooth Aster under a column of pink-tan specks.

Symphyotrichum ericoides.note: A bushy, much-branched plant with tiny needle-like leaves 1 to 2 cm, the branches lined on one side with crowds of small white daisies 1 cm across. Recorded with 8 cm leaves and 2.5 cm heads (the genus default). The model is thin stems with long grass blades and a haze of tan specks.

Symphyotrichum falcatum.note: A slender, grey-hairy, branching stem with small narrow leaves 2 to 4 cm, the branches lined with white daisies 2 cm across. Recorded with 8 cm leaves on a 35 cm plant, so the model is a rosette of sword blades like a yucca, with the flowers in a flat cap. The flower heads themselves read as white daisies, the best of the asters.

Symphyotrichum hesperium.note: A leafy stem with narrow lance leaves and pale lilac to white daisies 2 to 2.5 cm. The model is the same thin stem and tan specks as the other asters. Only six photographs, none of the whole plant, and two from Texas.

Symphyotrichum laeve.note: A bushy plant of smooth blue-green stems and clasping lance leaves, covered in late summer with dozens of violet-blue daisies 2 to 3 cm with yellow centres. The model's single leafy stem is right in kind. Its flowers are a thin haze of tiny tan and orange specks, not violet daisies; the plant does not read as in flower at all.

Symphyotrichum lanceolatum.note: Tall leafy stems in colonies with narrow lance leaves, the top a leafy pyramid of many white daisies 1.5 to 2 cm with yellow centres that redden. The model's stem and leaves are right in kind; in September the body is olive-brown, and the flowers are a few tan specks.

Symphyotrichum puniceum.note: A stout, bristly, purple-red stem to 1.8 m with clasping lance leaves, branching above into many blue-violet daisies 2.5 to 4 cm with 30 to 60 rays. The model is one thin green stem with a scatter of pale specks: no purple stem, no blue flowers.

Thalictrum dasycarpum.note: A big bushy plant to 1.8 m with purplish stems, leafy from bottom to top with blue-green leaves divided three or four times into small three-lobed leaflets, under large airy plumes of cream-white tassels. The model is a bundle of bare wires 1.8 m tall with a few tiny ladder leaves on the ground and dust at the top.

Thalictrum occidentale.note: A leafy woodland plant with thin, delicate leaves divided into many round three-lobed leaflets, and open panicles of nodding flowers: tassels of purple-brown stamens or small star-shaped seed clusters. The model is the same bundle of bare wires as the other meadow-rues.

Thalictrum venulosum.note: A knee-high leafy plant: blue-green leaves divided into many rounded, three-lobed leaflets with raised veins beneath, and loose panicles of small drooping tassels, greenish to purplish. The model is six bare wires from a few tiny ladders on the ground, with dust in the air.

Thermopsis rhombifolia.note: Low patches, a hand or two high: three-part leaves of broad grey-green leaflets with big leafy stipules; a short dense raceme of bright yellow pea flowers 2 cm at the top of each stem; curled, sickle-shaped pods. The model draws long ladder leaves of a dozen leaflets where the plant has three, and its flowers are loose yellow and orange chips.

Typha latifolia.note: A fan of long, flat, blue-green strap leaves to 2.5 m, twisting slightly, and a stiff round stalk with a dark brown sausage 10 to 18 cm long and 2 to 3 cm thick, a thinner spike above it that withers. The model reads as a cattail at once. It is one very narrow column where a clump spreads, and the spike is orange and outsized where it should be dark chocolate brown.

Urtica gracilis.note: Tall, unbranched, square stems in dense patches, with opposite, coarsely toothed, pointed leaves 7 to 15 cm, deeply veined, and drooping green-yellow strings of tiny flowers from the upper leaf joints. The model's tall stems with opposite leaves are right in kind; the leaves are small smooth ovals a third the size, and the hanging strings are missing.

Utricularia vulgaris.note: Free-floating feathery stems under the surface, finely branched and dotted with small dark bladders, and stout reddish stalks standing 10 to 20 cm out of the water, each with several bright yellow snapdragon-like flowers 1.5 to 2 cm with a rounded pouch. The model has a few blades on the water and yellow pinpoints: the flowers stand clear of the water and are the only part most people see.

Vaccinium myrtilloides.note: A low twiggy bush, knee high; small soft elliptic leaves 2 to 4 cm, velvety, red in autumn; clusters of small pink-white bells in May; blue berries with a pale bloom in clusters. The model has the height and blue berries, some floating outside it. The leaves are large flat plates (the same body as Western Snowberry); no flower shows in May.

Vaccinium oxycoccos.note: Thread-thin stems trailing over moss with tiny pointed leaves 0.5 to 1 cm, dark above and white beneath; nodding pink flowers on long red stalks, four petals swept straight back from a beak, like a shooting star; a red cranberry far larger than the leaves. The model is a mound of broad angular plates with a few specks: nothing thread-like, nothing tiny.

Veronica americana.note: Fleshy stems sprawling through shallow water and rooting as they go, with pairs of glossy, toothed, lance-oval leaves 2 to 5 cm, and loose racemes from the leaf joints of small violet-blue flowers with four lobes and a white eye. The model is a ring of specks on the ground and three bare wires half a metre tall, the same body as Northern Bedstraw; no flower shape is recorded.

Viburnum edule.note: A straggling slender shrub; opposite leaves with three shallow lobes, like a small maple leaf, red in autumn; small flat white clusters; red berries in small bunches. The model's leaves are plain plates in tiers on thick canes, the flowers float above it, and the berries it draws in August sit outside the plant.

Viburnum opulus.note: A tall shrub; opposite three-lobed maple-like leaves, red to purple in autumn; flat white lace-caps 8 to 10 cm across ringed with large sterile flowers; drooping bunches of bright red berries into winter. The model has plain dark plates on thick trunks, no flower in May, rust-brown rather than red leaves in September and no berries.

Vicia americana.note: A slender scrambling vetch with leaves of 4 to 8 pairs of narrow oval leaflets ending in a branched tendril, and loose one-sided racemes of 3 to 9 blue-purple to red-purple pea flowers 1.5 to 2 cm. It is recorded pale pink; the photographs are purple. The model's vine is a wisp at the host's foot.

Viola adunca.note: A small leafy tuft of oval to heart-shaped, round-toothed leaves on short stems, with blue-violet flowers 1 to 1.5 cm on stalks above them, the lower petal white at the base with dark lines and a hooked spur behind. The model is a mound of stacked plates with two flowers, half dark, on top; a plant in flower carries a dozen.

Viola palustris.note: A few round to kidney-shaped, scalloped leaves on separate stalks from a creeping stem in wet moss, and pale lilac to nearly white flowers 1 to 1.5 cm with dark purple veins on the lower petal. It is recorded the Early Blue Violet's blue. The model is the same stack of angular plates with three small dark flowers.

Viola rugulosa.note: A leafy plant a hand or two high: broad heart-shaped leaves on the stems as well as at the base, and white violets 2 cm across with a yellow throat and purple lines, held just above the leaves. It is recorded pink; every photograph is white. The model is a flat near-black rosette under 30 cm bare wires with small dark blobs at the tips.

Zizia aptera.note: A rosette of long-stalked, undivided heart-shaped leaves with scalloped edges, and stems with a few three-part leaves, each ending in a flat umbel 4 to 6 cm across of tiny bright yellow flowers. It is recorded pinnate; the basal leaf is a simple heart. The model is a tall ladder-leaf plant with umbels that read as dark flecks.
